extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IPR practitioners, patent prosecutors, and appellate counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Federal Circuit appellate review of PTAB inter partes review obviousness determinations, including claim construction, evidentiary sufficiency, and petition-defect issues. Focuses on standards of review, petition particularity requirements, and interplay of claim language and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the claims would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law. The court reviews the Board’s legal conclusion of obviousness de novo and its factual findings for substantial evidence. KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007) is controlling on obviousness principles (motivation to combine, common sense, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: ordinary meaning in light of the specification and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim terms by looking to their ordinary meaning in light of the specification and prosecution history (Phillips v. AWH Corp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may construe claims sua sponte when a dispute arises, provided it gives the parties notice and an opportunity to respond. Do not import limitations into claims that are not present in the claim language; consider specification and prosecution history to avoid constructions that exclude disclosed examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import unclaimed limitations absent support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be construed to add limitations that are simply not there; the claim language controls and the specification cannot be used to import limitations absent a clear basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if dependent claims or specification discuss a display relationship, the plain claim language controls. Rejection of constructions that would exclude examples disclosed in the specification is improper (see Verizon Servs. Corp. v. Vonage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-evidence review of Board factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual findings by the Board are reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may credit one expert over another if the testimony is supported by the prior-art disclosures and adequate explanation. 'Substantial evidence' can include supporting testimony tied to patents' figures and disclosures; conclusory assertions unsupported by the record are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity and claim-by-claim proof (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4); 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim and must address claim limitations with sufficient specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners cannot 'lump' together claims without addressing limitations unique to a challenged claim. The petitioner bears the burden to present a clear argument; the Board should not be required to 'decode' the petition to locate arguments. Failure to address a unique limitation may render the petition deficient as to that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-discretion standard for Board application of its regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Board decisions applying its own procedural regulations (e.g., deciding a petition is deficient under 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4)) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abuse of discretion may be found if the Board's decision rests on a legally erroneous interpretation of claim language or misapplies its regulations; but deference is given to the Board's procedural judgments otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of arguments not presented to the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments not raised to the Board are forfeited on appeal and generally may not be considered for the first time in the appellate proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-hoc attempts on appeal to raise additional arguments or to remedy petition defects will be rejected (Netflix; Intell. Bio-Sys. / Illumina guidance). Petitioners should present all claim-specific arguments before the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that different claim terms connote different meanings (but not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general presumption that the use of different terms or phrases in separate claims denotes different meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is rebuttable: different terms may be construed to cover the same subject matter where the context shows the patentee used different words to express similar concepts (Edwards Lifesciences; Nystrom; Ohio Willow Wood). The patentee must explain how an additional limitation changes the invalidity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When slightly different claim language does not create a new invalidity issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims 'use slightly different language to describe substantially the same invention,' the mere use of different words does not create a new issue of invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will treat substantially similar claim limitations as the same for invalidity analysis unless the patentee shows the additional words materially change the claim scope or analysis (Innova/Pure Water, Soverain Software).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal appropriate when corrected analysis yields only one permissible factual finding
rubrics_metrics.description: If correcting the Board's analysis results in 'only one permissible factual finding,' the appellate court may reverse the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Corning v. Fast Felt Corp.: when the record supports only one outcome after legal correction, reversal is appropriate rather than remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine and reliance on prior-art teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must show why an ordinarily skilled artisan would be motivated to combine the teachings of the prior art references to reach the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such motivation can be supported by express teachings in the references or expert testimony tying the references together; the petition should explain how combination addresses claim limitations (e.g., using Geva to supply intensity teachings in combination with Bird/Ishii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert testimony and tying it to patent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony is probative when it explains and ties opinions to the prior-art disclosures and figures rather than being conclusory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board is within its discretion to credit expert testimony that is supported by citations and adequate explanation; mere conclusory expert statements without connection to the record may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-away and record support
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that a prior-art reference 'teaches away' require evidentiary support in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cursory references to the record that lack substantive support do not establish that a reference teaches away from a combination; parties must point to specific teachings or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution-history amendments do not automatically import additional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment made during prosecution (e.g., adding a limitation such as 'outside the input area') does not necessarily establish relationships (such as coextensiveness with a display) unless the prosecution history clearly supports such a narrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be interpreted primarily from their language; prosecution history is relevant but courts will not read into claims limitations that the amendment record does not demonstrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition incorporation-by-reference limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporation by reference to other parts of the petition is permissible but does not relieve the petitioner of the obligation to present a clear, claim-specific showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a petitioner incorporates arguments made elsewhere in the petition, any limitation unique to a claim must still be addressed in a way that the Board can readily identify; mere placement of the claim in a grouped discussion is insufficient if the unique limitation is not substantively argued.
